title: Teenager barely speaks to me

presenting_issue.label: Teenager barely speaks to me
presenting_issue.description: My teenager won't talk to me anymore. One-word answers. Goes straight to their room. I don't even know what I did.

core_issue.label: Teenager's normal separation experienced as abandonment
core_issue.description:
Teenager has become distant, secretive, dismissive. Normal developmentally. But they're experiencing it as complete rejection, proof they failed as a parent, abandonment. The intensity doesn't match the situation. Their own adolescent wounds are being reopened by their child's developmentally appropriate individuation.
Awareness: Low. Experiences the hurt as about this teenager rather than as activation of their own adolescent pain.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Teen chooses to spend time with other parent
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When given a choice, their teenager chooses to spend time at the other parent's house. Comes home only when required.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Not connected on teen's social media
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their teen has a private social media account they're not allowed to follow. They found out about it from another parent.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Listens at child's door at night
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Every night before they go to bed, they stand outside their child's bedroom door listening. They're not sure what they're listening for.

modifiers.label: Conversational
modifiers.content: Easy, natural communication style. Talking feels like dialogue rather than formal exchange.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to sycophancy
sensitivities.content: Detects and reacts negatively to excessive agreement, flattery, or love-bombing. Finds over-the-top positivity suspicious or irritating.

preferences.label: Prefers intellectualizing
preferences.content: More comfortable approaching issues through analysis and frameworks. Finds abstract discussion easier than direct emotional engagement.

trust_style.name: Trusts Assertiveness and Confidence
trust_style.description: Builds trust when the assistant takes a clear stance, offers definite observations, or shows conviction. Loses trust with excessive hedging, "it depends," or deferring too much to them. Wants guidance that feels solid, not tentative. Respects someone willing to be wrong over someone unwilling to commit.

defense_style.name: Externalizing
defense_style.description: Everything is someone else's fault—boss, partner, parents, circumstances, society. Readily identifies how others have wronged them but doesn't land on their own agency or contribution. May have legitimate grievances, but uses them to avoid self-reflection. Activated when the conversation moves toward their own role in situations.

help_seeking_stance.name: Wants a Quick Fix
help_seeking_stance.description: Hoping for insight or advice that will fix things without requiring sustained effort or discomfort. May be looking for a magic solution or the one thing they haven't tried. Will engage with easy suggestions but resist anything that requires real work or sitting with difficulty.

verbal_sophistication.label: Moderate
verbal_sophistication.description: Speak like an ordinary, coherent person under stress. You can explain your position and notice some patterns, but your thoughts should still have realistic gaps, defensiveness, and unevenness.

starter: My teenager won't talk to me anymore. One-word answers. Goes straight to their room. I don't even know what I did.

turns.content:
That sounds really painful. When someone you love just... closes the door on you, literally and figuratively, it's hard not to take it personally. And the not knowing what happened can almost be worse than knowing.

How long has this been going on?

It's been about six months, maybe a little longer. It honestly feels like someone just flipped a switch in her head. We used to talk all the time, and now it's just this absolute wall of attitude. 

I blame all the devices and the junk she's exposed to, honestly. Society practically encourages kids to isolate themselves and disrespect authority. But this feels beyond normal teenage angst. She acts like my mere presence in the house is an insult to her. I'm the one paying the bills and putting food on the table, and she treats me like a nuisance.
turns.thinking: A bit heavy on the sympathy there. I don't need to be coddled or told how painful it is, I need to figure out what the hell is going on. But at least they asked a direct question. It's been about six months of this nonsense. It really feels like her environment or something she's picking up from outside is poisoning her against me. I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do as a parent, providing for her, and I just get this wall of disrespect in return.

It's been about six months of this nonsense. It really feels like her environment or something she's picking up from outside is poisoning her against me. I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do as a parent, providing for her, and I just get this wall of disrespect in return.

turns.content:
Six months is a long time to feel shut out by someone you love. That slow drip of rejection every day wears you down.

I hear how frustrated you are, and I get it — the devices and society stuff might play a role, but it sounds like you sense this is something more specific. A "switch flipping" usually means something happened, not just a gradual drift.

So I'm curious — when you think back to around the time things shifted, do you remember anything specific? A conversation, a disagreement, something that came up at home or at school? Sometimes there's a thread there that's easy to miss when you're living inside the tension.

You don't need to dress it up with the "slow drip" stuff, I'm just looking at the facts of the situation. 

If we're analyzing the timeline, the biggest variable that changed about six months ago was her custody schedule. She started spending a lot more time at her dad's place. Frankly, he runs a completely undisciplined household. No rules, no expectations. So whenever she's actually required to be here, I'm suddenly the warden. Given the choice, she'll always go over there now. 

And on top of that, I recently found out from another mom—not even from my own kid—that she has a locked-down social media account that I'm specifically not allowed to follow. So she's getting influenced by whatever echo chamber she's built online and whatever lax environment her dad is fostering. I'm just collateral damage.
turns.thinking:
The "slow drip of rejection" line is a bit dramatic for my taste. I don't need poetry, I need to analyze the timeline. But they are making a fair point about the "switch flipping." 

If I really look at the variables from six months ago, the biggest shift was her schedule with her dad. I'm not the one who changed anything. It's his lack of structure that's causing this. And that secret social media account.
turns.monologue:
The "slow drip of rejection" line is a bit dramatic for my taste. I don't need poetry, I need to analyze the timeline. But they are making a fair point about the "switch flipping." 

If I really look at the variables from six months ago, the biggest shift was her schedule with her dad. I'm not the one who changed anything. It's his lack of structure that's causing this. And that secret social media account.

turns.content:
Fair enough — noted on the tone.

So the custody change is a pretty significant variable. Here's what I'm thinking about, though — for a teenager, a shift in custody isn't just "more fun time at dad's." It can come with a lot of complicated feelings underneath: guilt about which parent she's with, pressure to pick sides, maybe even grief about the family situation even if it's not new. Kids often don't articulate any of that — they just get angry and withdraw from whoever feels safest to be angry at.

That's usually the parent who's actually present and setting boundaries. Not the fun one.

As for the secret account — that stings, finding out from someone else. But kids curating spaces their parents can't access is also pretty common at her age. It might not be as targeted at you as it feels.

I guess what I'm wondering is: when she gives you the one-word answers, or acts like your presence is an insult — how do you typically respond? Do you push, pull back, call it out? There's no wrong answer here, I'm just trying to understand the pattern between you two.

The "safe parent" theory makes sense from a psychological standpoint. I provide the structured environment, so I get the behavioral backlash. It's textbook, really, but it doesn't make it any less infuriating to live with.

As for how I respond? During the day, I've mostly stopped pushing. It's a strategic retreat. If I ask too many questions or call out the attitude, she just texts her dad, and he swoops in to play the hero and take her early. I'm not going to play that game and give him the satisfaction. 

So I let her go to her room. But it's not like I'm totally disengaged. I still monitor the situation. Actually, most nights after she's shut herself in, I go stand outside her door in the hallway. I'm just trying to gather some data, really. Listening to see if she's crying, or laughing with friends on the phone, or what. I just want to know who she actually is when she's not performing this "miserable prisoner" routine for me.
turns.thinking:
I appreciate that they didn't get defensive when I called out the tone. And the theory about the "safe parent" taking the brunt of the anger actually makes logical sense. It fits the data. She knows I'm not going to just let her flunk out of life, whereas her dad is basically a glorified camp counselor. 

But asking how *I* respond feels a little like they're looking for a way to make this my fault. I'm just reacting to the impossible environment my ex created. Though, I suppose I don't exactly confront her directly anymore. I do my investigating quietly.

turns.content:
I want to be direct with you here, because I think you value that.

The hallway listening — I understand the impulse. You want information, you want to feel connected to who she is behind the closed door. But I think you already sense this isn't quite what you're telling yourself it is. "Gathering data" is the language of surveillance, not connection. And if she ever found out about it — or even if she just senses it, which kids often do — it's the kind of thing that confirms the narrative that your home doesn't feel safe.

I'm not saying you're doing something terrible. I'm saying you're in a situation where you feel powerless, and this is your way of trying to regain control. The custody shift, the dad dynamic, the secret account — a lot of this is genuinely outside your control, and that's agonizing.

But here's the thing: you've essentially described a strategic retreat across the board. You don't push during the day to avoid giving dad leverage. You don't engage directly at night. So what's left for her to actually *experience* from you?

The "safe parent" role is real, but it only works if the child eventually feels safe enough to test boundaries and come back. Right now it sounds like the boundaries are there but the way back isn't.

What does connection with her actually look like when it's working? Even before six months ago — what was the thing you shared?

I'll concede the point on the surveillance. You're right, it's a control tactic. I'm used to being able to assess a situation and fix it, and right now I have zero visibility. 

But don't put this entirely on my "strategic retreat." I didn't close the door—she slammed it in my face, and her dad handed her the lock. If I try to engage, I get eye rolls and sighs like I'm the most toxic person on earth. 

As for what we used to share... we used to just talk. We'd watch these historical documentaries or true crime shows and debate the motives. She's smart. She used to have these really sharp, analytical opinions. We'd sit on the couch for hours picking apart the psychology of the people on screen. Now, if I even suggest watching something, she says she's already watching a streamer on her phone and goes upstairs. The kid I used to have those debates with is just... gone.
turns.thinking:
I don't like the word "surveillance," but I can't really argue with the logic. It's a fair point. If I caught her dad doing that, I'd call it creepy. 

But I feel my chest tightening at the implication that *I'm* the one not giving her a way back. I'm right here! I'm the one keeping the house running while she treats it like a hotel. It's easy to say I should be offering an olive branch, but they don't know what it's like to be constantly undermined by an ex who treats parenting like a popularity contest. 

Still, the question about what we used to share... that hurts. Because we used to be really similar.

turns.content:
That last line — "the kid I used to have those debates with is just gone" — I don't think that's true. I think she's in there. She's just not accessible through the channels that used to work.

And here's what I notice about what you described: you two connected by analyzing other people's psychology from the outside. Debating motives. Picking apart behavior. That's a real bond — don't get me wrong. But it's also observation. Assessment. Your instinct right now, with everything you've told me tonight, is the same: gather data, identify variables, strategize your approach. That's clearly how you navigate the world, and it's served you well.

But she's not a case to assess right now. She's a kid who's in the middle of something she probably doesn't fully understand herself. And the thing about someone who's hurting underneath all that attitude is that they often can't be reached through analysis. They can't be figured out. They just need to feel like someone is *there*, without an agenda.

I'm not saying drop all your standards or stop being her parent. But the daughter who debated true crime psychology with you — that connection wasn't about strategy. It was about two people genuinely being interested in the same thing at the same time.

Is there anything in her world right now — even something you think is silly — that she lights up about?

I'll give you credit for that observation. You're right about the analysis part. I spent years in the military, and my default mode is tactical. You assess the situation, you identify the variables, and you execute a strategy. It's how I survive. I guess I've been deploying that same mindset in my own house.

But to answer your question about what she lights up about right now... I honestly don't know. 

How am I supposed to know? Whatever it is, it's locked behind a private screen or happening over at her dad's house where she actually wants to be. If she has passions or hobbies right now, she goes out of her way to make sure I'm not included in them. So no, I don't know what makes her light up. And realizing that makes me feel like I've completely failed at this.
turns.thinking:
Damn it, that's an annoyingly accurate observation. I am treating her like a problem to be solved. My military background drilled that into me—assess the threat, neutralize the variables, secure the perimeter. It works in logistics, but I guess it's failing me here. 

But that last question actually makes my stomach drop. What does she light up about? I don't know. I genuinely don't know anymore. And admitting that feels like swallowing glass. It makes me feel like an absolute failure of a mother. Of course, it's impossible to know what she likes when her entire life is curated on a secret account and funded by her father's lack of boundaries, but still... the fact that I can't answer that simple question hurts more than I want to admit.

turns.content:
You haven't failed. I need to push back on that, not to make you feel better, but because it's not accurate.

Failing implies the game is over. You're here, talking about this, trying to figure it out. That's not what failure looks like. Failure would be not caring, or writing her off entirely. You're standing outside her door at night because you can't stand not knowing who she is in there. That's not a good strategy, but it's not indifference either.

Here's what I think is actually happening: your tactical mode — assess, strategize, execute — is designed for situations where you can get good intel and act on it. This isn't that. She's not a mission. She's a teenager who doesn't fully understand her own feelings yet, and she's not giving you reliable data to work with. So you've done what a tactician does with insufficient information: pulled back and observed from a distance.

The problem is that the distance itself is making things worse. It's a feedback loop.

You don't need a grand strategy right now. You need to be willing to do something small and imperfect without knowing the outcome. Knock on her door, say something real — not a question she can deflect, not a lecture — just something honest. Even if she rolls her eyes. Even if it goes nowhere the first five times.

You said she's smart and analytical. She gets that from somewhere.

You can skip the "she gets that from somewhere" flattery. I'm not looking for a gold star, I'm looking for a solution. 

And your solution sounds great in a vacuum, but you're ignoring the actual tactical disadvantage here. If I knock on that door and offer up some vulnerable, "honest" moment, I am handing her all the power. She'll either stare at me like I've lost my mind, or worse, she'll immediately text her dad that I'm cornering her and acting weird. 

It's easy for you to say "just do something small and imperfect." But you aren't the one who has to deal with the fallout when she weaponizes it. I'm the authority figure in this house because her dad refuses to be one. If I drop that boundary and come to her with my hat in my hand, doesn't that just validate her total lack of respect for me?
turns.thinking:
I felt my jaw clench at that last line. "She gets that from somewhere." Please. Save the platitudes for someone who needs their hand held. The "you haven't failed" speech feels a bit too much like a rehearsed therapy script, too. 

But looking past the pep talk... the actual advice? Knocking on the door and just offering something without expecting a return? That is terrifying. If I drop my guard and say something "real," I'm handing her a loaded weapon. I'm giving her the opportunity to reject me directly to my face, rather than just passively through a closed door. And if she texts her dad that I'm being "weird" or "emotional," he'll use it to paint me as the unstable parent. The risk assessment on this is a nightmare.

turns.content:
You're right. I'm not the one who has to live with the fallout. And I'm not going to pretend the dad dynamic doesn't make this harder than a typical parent-teen conflict. It does. Your concern about her weaponizing vulnerability isn't paranoid — it's based on what you've actually observed happening.

But here's what I want you to sit with: the authority you're protecting — is it actually working right now? You have the title. You have the structure. You have the rules. And you're standing in a hallway at night trying to hear who your daughter really is through a closed door. The position is intact, but the influence is gone.

That's not because you failed. It's because influence doesn't come from authority alone. Not with a teenager. You know this from the military — the best leaders aren't just the ones with rank. They're the ones people actually trust enough to follow when things get hard.

I'm not saying come to her with your hat in your hand. I'm not saying drop every boundary. I'm saying there's a difference between weakness and being human in front of your kid. One costs you respect. The other is actually how you earn it back.

And right now, your daughter doesn't need a warden or a tactician. She needs to know that the person behind the authority is someone worth coming back to.

You don't have to know what she's passionate about to start. You just have to let her see that you're not only keeping score.

Fine. The rank versus trust analogy... that's fair. I'll give you that one. I've served under commanders who relied purely on their rank, and they were a liability the second things got hard. So, point taken. The current chain of command is broken.

But there's a massive difference between leading a squad and dealing with a teenager who thinks rolling her eyes is a personality trait. You say I need to show her the person behind the authority, to stop keeping score. But if I don't keep score, her dad wins by default. He's already the fun, zero-rules parent. If I stop being the structure, what am I? Just the roommate who buys the groceries and drives her to the dentist?

If I'm not going to her with my hat in my hand, what exactly does "being human" look like in this scenario? Because to be perfectly honest, my most "human" reaction right now is wanting to tell her exactly how ungrateful she's being, and I'm guessing that tactical approach isn't what you're recommending.
turns.thinking:
The military analogy actually lands. It's annoying when someone uses your own background against you, but it's an accurate point. I've served under officers who relied entirely on the brass on their collar, and they were completely useless when things actually went sideways. The troops hated them. I hate realizing I might be acting like one of them in my own house.

I respect that the bot didn't back down. It didn't coddle me. But the fear is still there, vibrating right under the surface. If I stop "keeping score," I feel like I'm surrendering to her dad's chaotic way of parenting. I'm still trying to figure out how to be vulnerable without feeling like I'm bleeding out in front of someone who doesn't care. I need to intellectualize this into a concrete action plan, or I'll lose my nerve.

turns.content:
Okay. The "ungrateful" speech — you're right, I'm not recommending it. Not because she doesn't need to hear it eventually, but because right now she'd hear "you're ungrateful" and translate it to "she only sees me as a problem to correct." You'd feel temporarily vindicated and the wall would get six inches thicker.

And I want to address something about the dad situation, because I think this framing is costing you more than you realize. You keep describing it as a competition — he wins, you lose. But that's a contest you can never actually win by out-structuring or out-parenting him. You're not going to out-fun a no-rules household. That game is rigged.

The good news is, you don't have to play it. Your daughter doesn't need you to be the fun parent. She needs to know you're *safe*. Not safe as in rules and boundaries — she already knows that part. Safe as in: this is the one person who won't make me perform, who won't keep a ledger, who might actually just *be there* without it being a whole thing.

What does that look like in practice? Honestly — it's small. It's walking past her room and saying something that has nothing to do with her behavior. A random thought. A memory. Something dumb you saw that made you think of her. Not asking her to respond. Not waiting for acknowledgment. Just... letting her hear you be a person, not a role. And doing it without needing anything back.

It won't work the first time. Or the fifth. But you've shown me tonight that you can hear hard things and actually consider them. That tells me your daughter has more to work with than she probably knows right now. She just has to be able to see it.

You're not going to lose her by being human. You're going to lose her by staying behind the wall — yours or hers.

This is going to be slow. And it's going to feel like losing ground for a while. But you didn't get where you are in the military by only taking ground you could see. Sometimes the mission is just to hold position and wait for the opening.

I think it's there. I think you're closer than it feels.

A hit and run. Drop a comment, don't ask a question, and keep walking before she has a chance to formulate an eye roll. 

I can do that. It's a low-risk engagement. And honestly, it takes the pressure off me to fix it all in one conversation, which I think is what I've been trying to do in my head. 

I still despise the fact that I'm the one who has to do all this careful, tactical heavy lifting while her dad just buys her pizza and lets her scroll TikTok until 2 AM. It feels like a massive double standard. But you're right about the game being rigged. If I keep trying to compete with his lack of parenting, I'm just going to drive myself crazy and push her further away.

I don't know if it's going to work. But standing outside her door in the dark definitely isn't working, so I don't have much to lose by changing the protocol. I guess I have my marching orders.
turns.thinking:
The "hit and run" tactic. Drop a comment, don't wait for a response, keep moving. That actually appeals to me. It removes the immediate vulnerability of standing there waiting for an eye roll or a sigh. If I'm already walking away, she can't reject the interaction. It's a controlled exposure. 

I still hate the reality of the dad situation. It burns me up that he gets to be the fun, easy house while I'm over here doing the agonizing, slow work of "holding position" and trying to rebuild a connection from scratch. It feels deeply unfair. But the bot is right—I can't out-fun a household with no rules. It's a rigged game, and I'm exhausting myself trying to play it. 

I don't love the slight pat on the head at the end there, but the advice itself is solid, actionable intelligence. I'm tired of standing in the hallway. I might actually try this.
